On the Mild tariff, drivers all pay a more similar rate to charge, but that rate is always higher than on the Full or the Mild tariffs. If 2030 electricity prices are in line with our Low price scenario, and gasoline prices only increase with inflation, drivers on the Full and Medium tariffs would be able to fuel their cars at substantially lower prices than equivalent gasoline costs. On the Mild tariff, PG&E and SCE customers have ability to charge at close to gasoline parity, while SDG&E customers would have significantly higher fueling costs. However, if prices rise at a rate in line with our High price scenario, the more dramatic Full price profile is needed to ensure that the entire population of drivers is able to drive more cheaply on electricity than gasoline; while the Medium tariff can offer savings for some PG&E and SDG&E drivers, it will depend on their individual needs. Distribution of average annual EV charging costs when simulated population of drivers optimizes charging to 18 different price profiles. 4 Discussion 4.1 Non-marginal changes to system load This study presents a generous representation of load flexibility in response to prices. Flexibility is modeled across the entire customer base, for six major end uses, and assumes end uses are always available for price response (even EVs, which we assume can be charged at any time). Additionally, we use somewhat optimistic assumptions for how much load can be moved without disrupting the customer experience. Therefore, this study represents an upper bound of the flexibility that can be obtained across the analyzed end uses, and the magnitude of aggregate load response is quite significant. It is important to consider the impacts of such substantial changes in load. In small amounts, changes in demand can be considered “marginal”, and can help move the needle on dispatch of peaker plants, extreme market prices, and emissions. But at a certain magnitude, changes in customer load would fundamentally impact the way the grid would be built and operated. Energy market behavior, generation capacity build-out, and need and operation of front-of-the-meter resources like energy storage would be impacted. These changes would then lead to a substantial change in the cost of delivering energy to customers and would reshape the hourly dynamic prices that customers see. That would then lead to new results for load response, which would lead to new prices, and so on, until an equilibrium is reached. 54 While this study represents an upper bound of load response, it does indicate that such significant system load impacts may be possible,
